text.en: Which error number does SQL Server raise to the session chosen as a deadlock victim?

explanation.en: 1205 is the deadlock victim error. 547 is a constraint conflict, 2627 a unique/PK violation, 8152 string truncation.

example.en: Transaction (Process ID 57) was deadlocked on lock resources with another process and has been chosen as the deadlock victim.

text.en: What is the key difference between blocking and a deadlock?
Blocking resolves when the holder finishes; a deadlock is a cycle that SQL Server must break by killing a victim

explanation.en: Blocking is waiting; deadlock is circular waiting that can't resolve without intervention. The deadlock monitor detects cycles and rolls back one participant.

example.en: A long report holding locks blocks writers; two transfers updating accounts in opposite order deadlock.

text.en: Procedure A updates Orders then OrderLines; procedure B updates OrderLines then Orders. Deadlocks occur under load. What's the best structural fix?
Make both procedures access the tables in the same order

explanation.en: Opposite access order creates the classic cycle. Consistent ordering makes one transaction wait (blocking) instead of deadlocking. NOLOCK can't apply to updates; timeouts don't prevent cycles; the deadlock monitor can't be disabled.

example.en: Team rule: parent tables before child tables, ascending key order.

text.en: On SQL Server, where can you find recent deadlock graphs without configuring anything?

explanation.en: system_health runs by default and captures deadlock reports. Index usage stats, Query Store and the event log don't contain deadlock graphs by default.

example.en: SSMS → Management → Extended Events → system_health → filter name = xml_deadlock_report.

text.en: A session shows status 'sleeping', open_transaction_count = 1, and is the head blocker for 40 sessions. What's the likely cause?
The application began a transaction and never committed or rolled back (e.g. missing COMMIT or an unhandled error path)

explanation.en: A sleeping session with an open transaction holds its locks while doing nothing — an app bug (missing commit, exception path without rollback, user interaction inside a transaction). Use SET XACT_ABORT ON and proper error handling.

example.en: Short-term: KILL the session (its work rolls back). Long-term: fix the app's transaction handling.

text.en: Which three practices reduce deadlock frequency? (Select 3)
Access objects in a consistent order
Add indexes so statements touch fewer rows
Wait for user input inside the transaction

explanation.en: Ordering, short transactions and better indexes reduce lock overlap and duration. User interaction in transactions and SERIALIZABLE everywhere increase locks and deadlocks.

example.en: Also: RCSI for reader/writer conflicts and retry logic for the remaining 1205s.

text.en: A nightly batch job and the OLTP app occasionally deadlock. You prefer the batch job to be the victim. What do you set?
SET DEADLOCK_PRIORITY LOW in the batch job's session
SET DEADLOCK_PRIORITY HIGH in the batch job
SET LOCK_TIMEOUT 0 in the OLTP app

explanation.en: Lower deadlock priority makes the session the preferred victim. HIGH does the opposite; LOCK_TIMEOUT changes waiting behavior; NOCOUNT suppresses row-count messages.

example.en: The batch job should still retry on 1205.

text.en: Readers and writers deadlock frequently on a SQL Server database under locking READ COMMITTED. Which configuration change eliminates reader/writer deadlocks?

explanation.en: With RCSI, readers don't acquire shared locks, so they can't participate in lock cycles with writers. Writer/writer deadlocks can still happen.

example.en: Already default in Azure SQL Database.

text.en: Order the steps for handling a deadlock victim in application code.
Catch the exception and check for error 1205
Ensure the transaction is rolled back

explanation.en: Detect the deadlock, clean up, back off briefly to reduce re-collision, then retry the entire unit of work — not just the failed statement — with a retry limit.

example.en: EF Core: EnableRetryOnFailure handles transient errors including deadlocks for Azure SQL.

text.en: Which query rewrite makes WHERE YEAR(OrderDate) = 2026 SARGable?

explanation.en: A range on the raw column allows an index seek. Functions/casts on the column (b, c) and LIKE on a date (d) prevent seeks.

example.en: Half-open ranges (>= start AND < next start) also handle times correctly.

text.en: For each predicate on an indexed LastName column, answer Yes if it can use an index seek.

explanation.en: Leading literal prefixes and equality with matching types are SARGable. Leading wildcards and functions on the column force scans. With case-insensitive collations, UPPER is unnecessary anyway.

example.en: Need suffix search? Consider a persisted REVERSE(LastName) computed column with an index.

text.en: sys.dm_db_index_usage_stats shows an index with 0 seeks, 0 scans, 0 lookups but 3 million updates over a full business cycle. What should you do?
Consider dropping it — it only adds write overhead

explanation.en: An index never read but constantly maintained is pure cost. Confirm across a full cycle (the DMV resets on restart) and check it doesn't enforce a constraint before dropping.

example.en: Script it out first so it can be recreated if a rare report needs it.

text.en: A procedure with optional filters uses WHERE (@cust IS NULL OR CustomerId = @cust) AND (@from IS NULL OR OrderDate >= @from). It performs poorly for some parameter combinations. Which fix is commonly recommended?
Add OPTION (RECOMPILE) or build parameterized dynamic SQL with only the needed predicates

explanation.en: Catch-all queries get a single compromise plan. RECOMPILE lets the optimizer embed actual values and simplify predicates; dynamic SQL produces tailored, cached plans per combination.

example.en: Dynamic SQL must still use sp_executesql parameters to stay injection-safe.

text.en: Match each symptom to the most likely root cause.
Many sessions wait on LCK_M_X behind one sleeping session
Error 1205 in two procedures touching the same tables
Index scan on 50M rows for a single-customer lookup
Open transaction left by the app

explanation.en: Four common production problems and their typical causes.

example.en: Use DMVs to confirm before fixing.

text.en: In Azure SQL Database, how can you collect deadlock graphs for analysis?
Create an Extended Events session capturing xml_deadlock_report (e.g. ring buffer or event file target), or use diagnostic logs
Deadlocks can't be analyzed in Azure SQL

explanation.en: Azure SQL Database supports database-scoped Extended Events and exposes deadlock information through diagnostic settings. There's no OS event log, and sp_who2 doesn't show graphs.

example.en: CREATE EVENT SESSION deadlocks ON DATABASE ADD EVENT sqlserver.xml_deadlock_report ADD TARGET package0.ring_buffer;

text.en: A deadlock graph shows two sessions each holding an S lock on the same row and requesting X (conversion deadlock), from 'SELECT … then UPDATE' in one transaction. What prevents it?
Read the row WITH (UPDLOCK) so only one session can hold the update-intent lock
Split the UPDATE into two statements

explanation.en: UPDLOCK serializes the read-then-write pattern: the second session waits at the SELECT instead of deadlocking at the conversion. NOLOCK would read stale/dirty data; memory and splitting don't remove the cycle.

example.en: SELECT Qty FROM dbo.Stock WITH (UPDLOCK) WHERE Sku = @s; UPDATE dbo.Stock SET Qty = Qty - 1 WHERE Sku = @s;

text.en: A query filters WHERE Status = 'Open' OR CustomerId = 42, and separate indexes exist on each column, but the plan scans. Which rewrite often helps?
Split into two queries combined with UNION (or UNION ALL with de-dup logic) so each can seek

explanation.en: ORs across different columns can defeat single-index seeks; splitting lets each branch seek its own index (the optimizer sometimes does this via index union, but not always). Functions and NOLOCK don't help.

example.en: SELECT … WHERE Status='Open' UNION SELECT … WHERE CustomerId = 42;

text.en: An Azure SQL Database shows avg_cpu_percent at 98% for hours. Answer Yes or No.
Check Query Store for top CPU consumers before scaling up.
Scaling up vCores is a valid option if queries are already efficient.
Adding NOLOCK everywhere will reduce CPU usage significantly.

explanation.en: Tune first (top queries), scale when workload is genuinely efficient. NOLOCK affects locking, not CPU spent on scans/joins.

example.en: One missing index often drops CPU from 98% to 20%.

text.en: Which statement about the head blocker is correct?
It blocks others but is not itself blocked; resolving it unblocks the chain
It's always the session with the highest CPU

explanation.en: Blocking chains have a root: a session holding locks without waiting on anyone. It may be idle (sleeping) or running a long query.

example.en: Head blocker query: sessions in blocking_session_id values that don't themselves appear as blocked.

explanation.en: 1205 identifies deadlock victims. WAITFOR DELAY waits for a duration (WAITFOR TIME waits until a clock time; SLEEP isn't T-SQL). 2627 is a key violation that shouldn't be retried blindly.

example.en: Combine with SET XACT_ABORT ON in the procedure.

text.en: Three missing-index suggestions exist: (CustomerId) INCLUDE (Total), (CustomerId) INCLUDE (OrderDate), (CustomerId, OrderDate). What's the best action?
Create one consolidated index, e.g. (CustomerId, OrderDate) INCLUDE (Total)

explanation.en: Overlapping suggestions should be merged to cover the queries with one index, limiting write overhead. Blindly creating all of them multiplies maintenance cost.

example.en: Verify with the queries' plans after creating it.

text.en: Why do missing indexes increase both blocking and deadlocks?
Scans read and lock far more rows/pages than seeks, increasing lock overlap and duration

explanation.en: An UPDATE that scans 1M rows to change 1 must examine (and under locking isolation, lock) many rows; more locks held longer means more contention. Indexes narrow the footprint.

example.en: Indexing the WHERE column of a frequent UPDATE often fixes 'random' deadlocks.

text.en: Which two actions reduce blocking caused by a large nightly UPDATE on a busy table? (Select 2)
Process the update in small batches with separate transactions
Ensure an index supports the UPDATE's WHERE clause
Run it inside one huge transaction with SERIALIZABLE

explanation.en: Batches avoid lock escalation and long-held locks; indexes reduce rows touched. SERIALIZABLE and TABLOCKX maximize blocking.

example.en: UPDATE TOP (2000) … WHERE Processed = 0 in a loop.

text.en: Which statement terminates a blocking session and rolls back its open transaction?

explanation.en: KILL ends the session; its uncommitted work rolls back (which can take time without ADR). The other statements don't exist in that form.

example.en: KILL 57 WITH STATUSONLY shows rollback progress.

text.en: Why should foreign key columns usually be indexed?
Joins and parent deletes/updates must find child rows; without an index they scan the child table, causing slowness and blocking

explanation.en: FKs are valid without indexes, but parent operations and joins pay for scans. SQL Server doesn't create FK indexes automatically.

example.en: Deleting one customer scanned 100M orders until IX_Orders_CustomerId was created.

text.en: Answer Yes or No about deadlocks.
Deadlocks can be completely eliminated in any busy OLTP system with enough tuning.
The deadlock monitor usually picks the transaction cheapest to roll back as victim.
Deadlocks can involve resources other than locks, such as parallel query threads or memory.

explanation.en: You can minimize but rarely eliminate deadlocks, so retries are required. Victim selection considers DEADLOCK_PRIORITY, then rollback cost. Deadlocks can also involve intra-query parallelism and other resources.

example.en: Design for retry, not for perfection.

text.en: A .NET app passes a string parameter to a VARCHAR column filter and the query scans instead of seeks. What's the most effective fix in the app?
Specify SqlDbType.VarChar with the correct size for the parameter
Use string concatenation instead of parameters

explanation.en: .NET strings map to NVARCHAR by default; comparing NVARCHAR to a VARCHAR column converts the column (implicit conversion), blocking seeks. Matching the type fixes it. Concatenation causes injection and plan cache bloat.

example.en: In Dapper: new DbString { Value = s, IsAnsi = true, Length = 20 }.

text.en: Order the steps for resolving live production blocking.
Walk the chain to the head blocker and see what it's running
Decide: wait, or KILL the head blocker if safe
Fix the root cause (transaction scope, indexes, RCSI)

explanation.en: Observe, find the root, mitigate the incident, then prevent recurrence. Killing random blocked sessions doesn't help.

example.en: Capture the head blocker's SQL text before killing it for the post-incident review.

text.en: A statement waiting for a lock longer than 5 seconds fails with error 1222 instead of waiting indefinitely

explanation.en: LOCK_TIMEOUT bounds how long a statement waits; it raises error 1222. Note it cancels only the statement, not the transaction — handle it explicitly. It doesn't prevent deadlocks or affect other sessions.

example.en: Default -1 = wait forever.

text.en: An insert-heavy table with an IDENTITY clustered key shows PAGELATCH_EX waits on the last page under very high concurrency. Which feature targets this specific problem?
OPTIMIZE_FOR_SEQUENTIAL_KEY = ON on the index (or In-Memory OLTP for extreme cases)

explanation.en: Last-page insert contention is latch (not lock) contention; OPTIMIZE_FOR_SEQUENTIAL_KEY smooths it by controlling thread flow, and In-Memory OLTP eliminates latches. RCSI affects locking reads; hints and MAXDOP don't address latches.

example.en: ALTER INDEX PK_Events ON dbo.Events SET (OPTIMIZE_FOR_SEQUENTIAL_KEY = ON);

text.en: Match each wait or error to its category.
Blocked reader waiting for a shared lock
In-memory page latch contention (e.g. last-page inserts)

explanation.en: Know the signatures: deadlock 1205, lock timeout 1222, LCK_M_* lock waits, PAGELATCH_* in-memory latch contention (PAGEIOLATCH is disk IO).

example.en: PAGELATCH vs PAGEIOLATCH is a frequent trap.

text.en: A report query sorts 5M rows by OrderDate for one customer each time. Which index removes the sort?

explanation.en: With CustomerId first (equality) and OrderDate second, the rows for a customer are already ordered by date in the index — no sort needed. OrderDate alone requires filtering; Total is unrelated; hash indexes are unordered.

example.en: Equality columns first, then ORDER BY columns, then INCLUDE.

text.en: For each statement about statistics maintenance, answer Yes or No.
Outdated statistics can cause bad cardinality estimates and poor plans.
AUTO_UPDATE_STATISTICS should be turned off in most systems.
Index REBUILD updates that index's statistics with a full scan.

explanation.en: Statistics drive estimates; auto-update should stay on (optionally async). Rebuilding an index refreshes its statistics as if WITH FULLSCAN (REORGANIZE doesn't).

example.en: Skewed large tables may need scheduled UPDATE STATISTICS … WITH FULLSCAN.

text.en: Which approach reduces log-write saturation in Azure SQL Database caused by an app inserting rows one at a time with autocommit?
Batch inserts in explicit transactions or use bulk APIs/table-valued parameters

explanation.en: Each autocommit transaction forces a log flush; batching amortizes flushes. More indexes add log volume; NOLOCK and MAXDOP don't affect logging.

example.en: SqlBulkCopy or a TVP inserting 1,000 rows per call.

text.en: Which DMV shows currently held and requested locks?

explanation.en: dm_tran_locks lists lock resources, modes and request status (GRANT/WAIT). The others cover fragmentation, plans and system info.

example.en: SELECT request_session_id, resource_type, request_mode, request_status FROM sys.dm_tran_locks;

text.en: A vector search query is slow. The table has 5M rows with embeddings and no vector index; the query uses VECTOR_DISTANCE in ORDER BY with TOP 10. Which two actions improve latency? (Select 2)
Create a DiskANN vector index and query with VECTOR_SEARCH (TOP … WITH APPROXIMATE)
Apply selective relational filters first (e.g. category) to reduce candidates when exact search is required
Add a B-tree index on the vector column

explanation.en: Exact search computes distance for every row; an ANN index (DiskANN) avoids that. If exact results are required, reduce the candidate set with selective predicates. Vector columns can't be B-tree keys, and NOLOCK doesn't reduce computation.

example.en: CREATE VECTOR INDEX vix ON dbo.Docs(Embedding) WITH (METRIC = 'cosine', TYPE = 'diskann');

text.en: A procedure calls sp_invoke_external_rest_endpoint inside a transaction that also updates rows. Users see long blocking. Why?
Locks from the updates are held while waiting for the external HTTP call to finish
HTTP calls lock the whole database

explanation.en: External calls add unpredictable latency; inside a transaction they extend lock duration. Call external services outside transactions (or asynchronously) and keep transactions short.

example.en: Get the embedding first, then open a short transaction to write the result.

text.en: Complete the batched delete that avoids lock escalation.

explanation.en: DELETE TOP (n) limits each batch below the ~5,000-lock escalation threshold; @@ROWCOUNT = 0 ends the loop. LIMIT/FIRST aren't T-SQL; @@ERROR and @@TRANCOUNT measure other things.

example.en: Support the WHERE clause with an index on LoggedAt.

text.en: A query uses COUNT(*) > 0 to check whether matching orders exist. What's the more efficient pattern?
SELECT * and count rows in the app

explanation.en: EXISTS can stop at the first match; COUNT(*) must count all. Returning rows to the app or using cursors is far worse.

example.en: IF EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM dbo.Orders WHERE CustomerId = @c) …

text.en: A deadlock graph shows a single session with multiple threads (exchange event / parallel query) deadlocking with itself. What's a common mitigation?
Reduce parallelism for that query (MAXDOP hint) and/or improve indexing to avoid large parallel scans

explanation.en: Intra-query parallelism deadlocks involve parallel threads; lowering DOP or giving the query a cheaper plan (seek instead of big parallel scan) avoids them. Other options make things worse or are impossible.

example.en: Apply via Query Store hint: OPTION(MAXDOP 1) for that query.

text.en: Which practice keeps transactions short in application code?
Do all reads/validation and external calls before BEGIN TRAN; include only the necessary writes inside
Open the transaction when the user opens a form

explanation.en: Minimize the time locks are held: prepare outside, write inside, commit quickly. Long-lived and user-driven transactions are blocking factories.

example.en: Validate inventory and call the payment API first; then a 5 ms transaction writes the order.

text.en: For each statement about indexing strategy, answer Yes or No.
More indexes always improve overall performance.
Equality columns should usually precede range columns in a composite key.

explanation.en: Indexes cost writes and storage; balance is key. Equality-then-range order maximizes seek selectivity, and covering indexes avoid lookups.

example.en: (TenantId, CreatedAt) INCLUDE (Status, Total).

text.en: Which Azure SQL tier change best addresses a database that is efficient but consistently limited by log write throughput and needs to grow beyond 4 TB?

explanation.en: Hyperscale supports very large databases (up to 128 TB) with high log throughput and fast scaling. Basic is tiny; serverless targets intermittent use; fewer vCores reduces capacity.

example.en: Tune first — tier changes are for genuinely efficient workloads hitting limits.

text.en: Match each problem to the most targeted fix.
Reader/writer deadlocks under locking READ COMMITTED

explanation.en: Different deadlock patterns need different fixes; recognizing the pattern from the graph is the skill.

example.en: All patterns still need retry logic.

text.en: Which index design suits a table queried mainly by WHERE IsActive = 1 (5% of rows) and ORDER BY Name?
A filtered index on (Name) WHERE IsActive = 1, including needed columns

explanation.en: A filtered index stores only active rows already ordered by Name — small and directly useful. A bit-column index is unselective; columnstore targets analytics.

example.en: CREATE INDEX IX_Active_Name ON dbo.Users(Name) INCLUDE (Email) WHERE IsActive = 1;

text.en: Why might a query using a scalar UDF in the SELECT list over millions of rows be slow on older compatibility levels?
The UDF executes row by row and prevents parallelism; scalar UDF inlining (compat 150+) can fix eligible UDFs

explanation.en: Non-inlined scalar UDFs run per row and serialize the plan. Upgrading compatibility or rewriting as inline expressions/TVFs helps.

example.en: Check sys.sql_modules.is_inlineable.

text.en: Which two signals suggest an index should be added? (Select 2)
A frequent query scans a large table to return a handful of rows
Key lookups execute thousands of times for a hot query
The table is written constantly and rarely read
The query already performs a covering seek

explanation.en: Large scans for few rows and repeated lookups point at missing or non-covering indexes. Write-heavy, read-rare tables and already-covered queries don't need more indexes.

example.en: Weigh read benefit vs write cost for every new index.

text.en: With Accelerated Database Recovery enabled, what changes when you KILL a session that ran a huge update for an hour?
Rollback completes almost instantly instead of taking about as long as the work done

explanation.en: ADR's persistent version store allows logical revert, so rollbacks no longer replay the entire log. Work is never committed by KILL.

example.en: Without ADR, KILL WITH STATUSONLY may show hours of remaining rollback.

text.en: Analyze their plans and missing-index hints
Design consolidated indexes and test write impact
Deploy and verify, dropping unused indexes over time

explanation.en: Start from measured hot spots, understand plans, design deliberately, then validate and prune.

example.en: Repeat after major releases.

text.en: After enabling optimized locking in Azure SQL Database, which benefit should you expect for a workload with many concurrent single-row updates on different rows?
Less lock memory, fewer lock escalations and reduced blocking between updates on different rows
Elimination of all writer/writer conflicts on the same row

explanation.en: TID locking and LAQ reduce held row locks and blocking for updates on different rows. Two writers on the SAME row still conflict. It's unrelated to backups or indexing.

example.en: Check with SELECT DATABASEPROPERTYEX(DB_NAME(), 'IsOptimizedLockingOn');
